lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: "Macs don't get viruses" is a myth defenders still meet. Information stealers such as Atomic Stealer (lesson 16) have been sold to criminals as a monthly service since 2023, and Microsoft documented new campaigns delivering them to Macs in 2026. The built-in controls are strong, but they mostly decide what may *launch*; social engineering goes around them.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
md: Do not expect an attacker's password prompt, curl URL or file path to show up in plain text in the unified log. Default privacy redaction hides many dynamic strings. Plan on Endpoint Security or EDR telemetry for process command lines, and use the unified log for subsystem state changes.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
md: A clean malfind proves little too. Code injected into an EXECUTE_READ region with a properly mapped file, or code that hides its pages while sleeping (lesson 12), will not match these rules. Use malfind with the other views, never alone.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: The call stack: frames, return addresses and saved frame pointers
md: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so people often assume an overflowing array also spills downward. It does not. `strcpy`, `gets` and loops write from `buf[0]` toward `buf[7]` and beyond, which means toward *higher* addresses: straight into the saved frame pointer and the return address of the same frame.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: Re-ID is open-set retrieval: open-set means the people at test time are not among the training classes. You do not predict a label; you learn distances that rank true matches first for people the model has never seen.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: Misconception: "warm-up makes a benchmark more accurate". It makes it measure **steady state**. If your function really runs once per request on cold caches, the warmed number is precise and wrong. Decide which regime production is in, then measure that one.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Launching and watching a Miles run
md: Architecture flags are not self-validating. Two checkpoints of one family can ship a different `--rotary-base`, vocab padding or norm epsilon. Diff the checkpoint's `config.json` against its file in `scripts/models/` before a first run and append any drifted value, for example `--extra-args "--rotary-base 10000"`.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
md: Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
md: **Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
md: Give Muon the hidden 2D matrices (Q, K, V kept separate), AdamW everything else. In PyTorch that is two optimizers stepped together. Distributed, Muon costs one extra bf16 gather per matrix and every rank's Newton-Schulz on the full matrix, against one fewer state buffer than AdamW.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
md: Every stable parametrization is, at large width, either a kernel machine with frozen features or a feature learner. muP is the feature learner in which every layer moves as much as stability allows: that is what "maximal update" means.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
md: muP transfers across width; depth needs a branch rule; the token horizon needs an LR correction (about $D^{-0.32}$ at large scale); weight decay needs its $\eta\lambda$ timescale held fixed; regularization needs retuning.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: Choosing a lock: in application code use the standard mutex, which is already uncontended-fast and spin-then-sleep. Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, or sharding: splitting the data into parts that each have their own lock) before tuning spin counts.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
md: When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Responses: naming, indictments, sanctions and disruption
md: Do not assume a response worked because it happened. Indicted officers keep working from home; sanctioned groups keep stealing; botnets are rebuilt from new unpatched devices. Measured effects are rarely public, and even the UK's NCF says measuring the effect of covert operations "is often very hard". Report what was done, and what is known about what changed.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running for real: metrics, checkpoints, export and a multi-node recipe
md: In all three published runs generation takes about half the step or more. Read your own `timing/train/` split before tuning: if generation dominates, the levers are vLLM parallelism and memory (lesson 4), non-colocated async generation (lesson 5) and response length, not the training backend.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
md: A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
md: Routing is decided hop by hop from tables, and the most specific matching prefix wins. On the internet those tables are built from announcements other networks make, which BGP accepts on trust unless someone filters or validates them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system (one that, like an FTL, appends every write to a log and cleans it, but knows which files were deleted), the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Sparse data: how a few ratings re-identified Netflix users
md: In sparse, high-dimensional data, every person is an outlier. A handful of rare facts, even noisy ones, is enough to find a record, and then the whole record is exposed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Never let users re-run a noisy query for free. Repeated noisy answers can be averaged; composition counts every one. Cache answers or charge each run to the budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
md: Do not treat LINDDUN as a compliance checklist. Its value is the same as STRIDE's: asking each element and flow "how could this hurt the people in the data?" before the design is fixed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise
md: A privacy review asks, in order: what data actions happen, how they could hurt people (LINDDUN), whether the processing is necessary (DPIA), what must leave the system and the matching technique (DP, PSI, secure aggregation, or not releasing), how the design minimises, and how rights reach every copy.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021: about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Linux runs, on each CPU, a task that has not had more than its weighted fair share: CFS picks the smallest vruntime; EEVDF picks, among eligible tasks (lag of zero or more), the earliest virtual deadline. Nice values set weights 1.25x apart; slices end on ticks and wakeups, and those are your involuntary switches.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them
md: Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: Misconception: "we validate all input, so we are safe". Format checks (is it an integer, is it a known product) do not test meaning (is this quantity possible, is this step allowed now, has this coupon been used). Logic flaws live in the meaning.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Starbucks gift cards and two browser sessions (2015)
md: Protect the resource being spent, not the path to it. A one-time flag in the session, a disabled button or a cleared form all guard one route to the balance; a lock or atomic update on the balance itself guards every route.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: Write the invariant first, then a test that tries to break it in every way this course showed: odd values, odd order, and many at once. A test suite with no parallel test cannot fail on a race.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
md: Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
md: Joining hypervisors, backup servers and RMM consoles to the production domain feels tidy, but it gives whoever owns AD the keys to everything at once. Separate authentication for these systems is the single design choice that most often decides whether a domain compromise becomes a business-ending outage.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
md: Every reward-side fix encodes an assumption about *where* the reward is wrong: in members' disagreement, in label noise, in a named feature, or in extreme values. Hacks that live outside that assumption pass straight through, so these methods complement an outside check; they do not replace it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Variable-length sequences on the trainer: packing and balance
md: Variable lengths waste trainer compute three ways: padding inside a row, empty rows, and idle ranks. Pack rows (with `cu_seqlens`), balance tokens across ranks, and normalize the loss by the global token count so none of this changes the gradient.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100, NVIDIA's 2017 data center GPU (125 TFLOP/s of Tensor Core math over about 900 GB/s, a ridge of 138.9), to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask (the set of CPUs a task may run on, set with `sched_setaffinity()`).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: Misconception: once a task is in a custom DSQ it is on its way to a CPU. It is in your custody until dispatch moves it, and a property change can pull it back out through `ops.dequeue()` at any time.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Vaults: one place to store, control and audit secrets
md: A vault concentrates risk. CircleCI was, in effect, a vault for its customers' deploy secrets. Narrow policies per workload, short-lived tokens, audit logs shipped elsewhere, the ability to seal fast, and a root of trust in a KMS or HSM are what make the concentration worth it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
md: Trace by hand: mark the source, follow every assignment and call, and stop at each sink. A function only counts as a sanitizer if its output is safe for that specific sink, whatever the input. Rewriting or deleting bad patterns almost never qualifies.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
md: Parameterising user data protects you only if the component never interprets the final string. When reviewing a feature that adds interpretation (lookups, templates, expressions, fetching URLs) to a widely used API, treat every caller's data as reaching that new sink.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
md: Memory-safety policy is now a review topic: new memory-unsafe code needs a reason, unsafe blocks in Rust get the most scrutiny, and old C and C++ keeps its hardening. Android's data says the payoff comes from new code, because vulnerabilities concentrate in recent changes.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
md: Everything in the KEXINIT lists is negotiated in the clear and only later authenticated through the exchange hash. Anything the hash does not cover (extra messages, the implicit sequence numbers) is a place where an active attacker can interfere.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
md: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Integrity: no read down, no write up. If you remember which way information is allowed to flow, you can rebuild both rule sets.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
md: A proxy only protects an application if it is the only way in and the application can tell the difference. Signed, audience-bound assertions let the application check for itself.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
md: Pace all workers with one shared limiter, honour Retry-After and the reset headers, back off exponentially with full jitter, retry only idempotent calls and only at one layer, and report partial failures item by item.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: A hash only proves integrity if the expected fingerprint reached you over a channel the attacker cannot touch. If an attacker can change both the message and the published hash, the check passes. Fixing that needs authenticity: a digital signature (or a keyed hash) that only the real sender can produce. The cryptography course covers these.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
md: CVSS = how bad in theory. KEV = being used now. EPSS = likely to be used soon. Combine them with what *your* asset is and how exposed it is. A score without context is not a priority.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Rules of thumb that keep you on the right side: test only systems you own or have written permission to test; stay inside the agreed scope (systems, dates, methods); stop and report the moment you see other people's data; never keep or share it. A bug bounty programme's published rules are a form of written permission, but only for what they list.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Budgets: what security costs and how to ask for money
md: Weak argument: "the average breach costs USD 4.99 million, so give us 1 million." The average is not your loss, the board knows it, and the request names no risk and no result. Strong argument: "this USD 250k removes an estimated 700k of expected annual loss from ransomware on our order system, according to our FAIR model with these ranges."

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: The operating model: decision rights, incentives and culture
md: Write down who decides (one Accountable per activity), make the secure way the easy way, give teams a clear intake with service levels, and align incentives with security outcomes. Culture shows in which priority wins when they conflict.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
md: Do not soften the verdict to keep a client happy, and do not dramatise it to be noticed. Both destroy the summary's main asset: that the reader can take it at face value. If the news is good, say so plainly; a calibrated "the defences held" is as useful as a warning.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Each method buys information somewhere. V-STaR gets more out of the answer key by learning from failures; SCoRe uses the answer key to reward fixes; Meta-Rewarding has no outside signal, so it can only exploit its own generation-verification gap, which Song et al. saw shrink to about zero within a few rounds on math.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Evaluate compression like a model change: measure your task metric at several ratios on your own data, and measure end-to-end latency including the compressor. The published gains were measured on specific benchmarks with specific target models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
md: Equifax, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon (lesson 14) and MOVEit all ended the same way: a **web shell** written into a directory the web server executes. Two cheap controls hit all of them: make web roots read-only to the app's own user, and alert on new script files appearing there.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
md: In SGLang a grammar costs three things: a compile per distinct schema (hidden by the cache after the first request), a CPU mask per request per step (hidden behind the forward pass by delaying only the sampling), and one decode step per forced token.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Fully async needs separate rollout and training GPUs to overlap anything, and its README lists no evaluation mode (it would conflict with the continuously running model), so evaluate with a separate path or job. Importance-sampling corrections such as TIS (lesson 8) help with mismatch, but the docs say they do not justify an unlimited stale queue.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Consensus under attack: Sybil, 51 percent and eclipse attacks
md: Open networks defeat Sybil attacks by making votes cost a scarce resource (work or stake). The attacker's share sets the odds; confirmations and finality are how recipients buy safety.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Front-running, MEV and commit-reveal
md: Commit-reveal hides choices, not existence: observers still see that you committed and when. Without a reveal deadline and a rule for non-revealers (for example, forfeiting a deposit), a participant who dislikes the outcome can simply never reveal.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
md: The CSRB's review of the group known as Lapsus$ found that, in a few cases, the attackers "impersonated help desk personnel over direct chat messages and encouraged employees to approve the MFA prompts". When you contact a user about an alert, use a channel the attacker cannot be sitting in, and teach users that the real SOC never asks them to approve a prompt.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics
md: The analyst's job, in one sentence: answer each alert with evidence, quickly and in order of risk, write it down so others can act and check, and use the access that makes this possible only for that purpose.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
md: People outside your organisation (carrier staff, outsourced agents, contractors) can be the weak link for your accounts. Design so that no single outside person's mistake or bribe hands over a login, and make reporting approaches normal inside.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one. Lesson 5 shows how a latent gets its name and how that name is tested.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$, where norm rescales to sum to 1. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction: the kernel moves in-use pages around to assemble a free contiguous run. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
md: LLM judges are convenient but not neutral. CAA used GPT-4 to score open-ended answers from 1 to 10 and notes the scores are sensitive to the rubric's wording; they spot-checked against their own ratings. String-matching refusal detectors have the opposite problem: they catch "I'm sorry" but not a harmful reply, so Arditi et al. paired them with Llama Guard 2.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: One layer: attention adds a cross-position change, add & norm, the FFN adds a per-position change, add & norm. At inference the encoder runs once and the decoder runs once per output token, with beam search choosing among the most probable partial outputs.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
md: BM25 only matches the terms you typed, after analysis. A document saying "low-cost airfare" scores 0 for cheap flights. Synonyms, stemming, query expansion (adding related terms to the query), or a dense retriever (a neural network maps query and documents to vectors, ranked by vector similarity) are needed for vocabulary mismatch, which is why many systems combine BM25 with vector search.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices $f(x)\,dx$. To evaluate one, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the ends; when no antiderivative is available, add up trapezoids numerically.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
md: The Jacobian generalizes the derivative to vector outputs, and the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians. Backprop never forms those matrices: it carries one row (the loss gradient) backward and multiplies it into each layer's Jacobian, giving $W^\top$ products for inputs and outer products for weights.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: `if`, `while`, `&&` and `||` all branch on an exit status. `[` and `test` are commands that turn a comparison into a status. Functions return a status with `return` and data on standard output.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth breaking. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to flush buffered output, remove lock or temporary files, or stop its own child processes, which can be left running as orphans. Send SIGTERM, give it a few seconds, then escalate.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
md: More GPUs do not automatically mean lower latency. Pipeline and data parallelism add capacity and throughput but leave single-request latency where it was, and tensor parallelism hits a floor set by per-layer communication latency.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction. The flow breaks on dependencies on recent results and on jumps the predictor gets wrong; a misprediction costs roughly the pipeline's length in cycles.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A null pointer or an uninitialized pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is *undefined behavior*: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. Often you get a crash (a segmentation fault on Linux: the process touched an address with no memory mapped there, so the operating system kills it), but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so do not rely on a crash to tell you.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
md: Never touch a node after freeing it, and that includes reading its next field to continue a loop. Save every pointer you still need from a block before you free the block.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
md: On the Mac used for this course, the ASan runtime in Apple's clang refused leak detection: running with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1` printed `detect_leaks is not supported on this platform`. On Linux, ASan's leak check is on by default. Check leaks where your tools support them, for example in Linux CI.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
md: A thread gets values by ownership: `move` them into its closure, `send` them through a channel, get them back from `join`. Since every value has one owner, two threads cannot both reach it unless a type built for sharing is in between.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: `A * B` in NumPy and PyTorch is the **element-wise** (Hadamard, after the mathematician Jacques Hadamard) product, which multiplies entries in matching positions, not matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is `A @ B` (or `np.matmul`). With two same-shape square matrices both run without error and give different answers, so this bug is silent.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Tensors are arrays with any number of axes; `@` multiplies the last two and broadcasts the rest. Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, and sizes must be equal or 1. Name the axis a reduction removes, and keep it with `keepdims=True` when you broadcast back.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches: noisy gradients and the training loop
md: SGD steps on an unbiased but noisy gradient estimate from a minibatch. Noise falls only as $1/\sqrt B$, so moderate batches with many steps are usually the efficient choice.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Early stopping and why big models still generalize
md: Gradient descent fits high-curvature, smooth directions first and nearly flat, wiggly ones last. Noise lives mostly in the flat directions, so stopping at the best validation error keeps the signal and skips the noise. That is why early stopping acts like an L2 penalty.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
md: A ReLU hidden unit is a hinge (one input) or a cut with a ramp (many inputs). The output layer adds these up into a piecewise-linear function, and equivalently, it runs a linear model on the features the hidden layer computed.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch
md: Gradients accumulate across calls too. In this engine, `backward()` resets only the output's grad, so calling it twice on `f = x * x` with `x = 3` leaves `x.grad` at 12, not 6. That is why part 3 zeroes every parameter's grad before each backward pass, and why PyTorch training loops call `opt.zero_grad()`.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: A page fault is not a bug. It is a legal access to a page that happens not to be in memory, and the program never notices except as a delay. A segmentation fault is different: an access to an invalid page, which the OS treats as an error.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
md: Directories map names to inode numbers; inodes map file offsets to disk blocks; the per-process descriptor and the open file table remember where you are. Path lookup costs disk reads in proportion to the path's depth unless the cache has the blocks.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML with a classifier on a rare class. Its **recall** is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$, the sensitivity, and does not depend on the base rate; its **precision** is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$, the posterior, and does. High recall can still come with mostly false alarms.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: One matrix, Sigma, holds every pairwise covariance. Any weighted sum has variance a-transpose Sigma a, and a Gaussian with covariance Sigma is just mu + L z with independent standard normals z.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Before launching, choose alpha, power and the minimum effect worth detecting, then compute n. Do not stop early on a peek unless the method allows it, and report the effect with its interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
md: Misconception: Kaplan's power laws were wrong. The loss-versus-size and loss-versus-data trends were real and still hold in shape. What shifted was the **compute-optimal allocation** derived from them, which is sensitive to experimental details. A scaling law is only as good as the runs it was fitted on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, online tests
md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Misconception: a higher similarity score means a more relevant passage across queries. Cosine scores are only comparable within one query's ranking and one model. A fixed threshold like 0.7 that works for one model can be meaningless for another.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: A byte-level BPE tokenizer is three small functions: train (count pairs, merge the top one, mint ids from 256), encode (apply merges by lowest id) and decode (join bytes, decode UTF-8 with errors replaced). The regex split adds one rule: count and merge inside chunks only.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
md: Adam's step is about **lr in size regardless of gradient scale**. That is its strength, and also why L2 regularization inside Adam misbehaves. Use AdamW when you want weight decay with an adaptive optimizer.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric. If your embeddings are not unit-length, an inner-product index ranks differently from cosine. Faiss (Meta's open-source vector search library) documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1. Cosine is the inner product divided by both lengths, so when both lengths are 1 the two are equal.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
md: Blocking install scripts stops code that runs at install time. It does not stop malicious code that runs when your app imports the package, or a `.pth` file that Python runs on start-up. It removes the easiest path, not every path.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
md: Malicious dependency equals intrusion. Scope by version and time window, contain, assume every machine that ran it is compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, hunt, rebuild, then fix the control that failed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Verification is the fix: why filtered self-training does not collapse
md: The generator does not have to be right; the kept set has to be. Collapse is avoided when a verifier keeps more correct than incorrect examples, and its judgments must track this generator's actual errors.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: `mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SS7: a signalling club that stopped being a club
md: The common mistake is to look for a bug to patch. SS7 location tracking and SMS redirection use messages exactly as specified. The fix is deciding who may send which message about which subscriber, at the network edge.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM swaps and port-outs: an identity problem, not a radio problem
md: A phone number is an account at someone else's company. Carriers must verify people before moving numbers; everyone else should treat a recent SIM change as a red flag and stop letting SMS alone prove identity.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a telecom and space defence map
md: Telecom and space systems fail in the same way: trust given to whoever can reach an interface. Bind every claim to an authenticated peer, check that requests make sense for their subject, encrypt hops you do not control, and audit what the system really does.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Build a TTT-Linear layer: inner loop, dual form and outer gradient
md: Write the inner gradient as a formula and the whole TTT layer is ordinary autograd: the dual form is the primal form reordered into matmuls (equal to 1e-15), and backprop through time costs activation memory linear in $T$. On recall, $b = 1$ beat larger blocks in every run; how $b = 16$ compares with the whole sequence changed with the seed, so one run cannot rank them.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
md: Two magazines per CPU, one loaded and one previous, guarantee that after every depot trip the CPU holds one full and one empty magazine. That alone bounds depot traffic at 1/M for any workload. Without the previous magazine, an alloc-alloc-free-free loop can send half of all calls to the depot.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
md: Every network hunt has benign twins. Software update agents and monitoring tools beacon perfectly regularly; some applications connect to fixed IP addresses by design; content delivery networks make 'rare destination' lists long. Attackers add **jitter** (random variation in the check-in interval) precisely to raise the CV. Combine signals (regular, rare, no DNS, unusual process) rather than trusting one.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Indicators: types, life cycle and decay
md: Every indicator needs a source, a first-seen and last-seen date, and a confidence. Load it, watch what it matches, and retire it on a schedule that fits its type: days for phishing domains, longer for behaviours.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
md: Threat modeling happens at design time and keeps happening. A threat model is maintained alongside the system and refined as it changes, not written once for an audit.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
md: Principles pull against each other. Separation of privilege adds steps that strain psychological acceptability; least privilege adds roles that strain economy of mechanism. Saltzer and Schroeder call them warnings, not rules: when you violate one, write down why the trouble is accounted for.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: Symptoms of thrashing: `pgdemote_*` and `pgpromote_success` both climbing fast at the same time. Pages are moving down and back up. Either the hot set is larger than DRAM, or headroom is too small. Migration itself consumes memory bandwidth on both tiers.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The TLS 1.3 handshake, message by message
md: Two messages carry the security: the **key shares** create a secret no eavesdropper can compute, and **CertificateVerify** ties that secret to the certificate's key. Without the signature, a man in the middle could run one DH exchange with each side.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: CUDA: *scalar program, blocked threads*. Triton: *blocked program, scalar threads*. In Triton you think about which tile each program owns; the compiler thinks about which thread holds which element.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
md: Misconception: "sharing a vocabulary makes images and text equally easy to model." Image tokens have very different entropy (the average surprise of the next token, $-\sum p \log p$: high when many tokens are about equally likely) from text tokens, and the paper attributes the instability exactly to modalities of different entropy sharing one softmax.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
